Immune Response to Chronic Pain
in Murine Spleen

TissueMurine Spleen
StainingHematoxylin & Eosin (H&E)
AnalysisImageJ · Jupyter Notebook
StatisticsOne & Two-Tailed t-Tests
Project Overview

This study investigated how chronic pain affects the immune system by examining germinal center morphology in murine spleen tissue. The spleen plays a central role in immune response — it filters blood, removes pathogens, and hosts germinal centers where B cells proliferate and produce antibodies.

Four mouse spleen samples were dissected and sent to histology for processing. Two mice were uninjured controls (saline injection) and two were injured (chronic pain model via MIA injection). Samples were deparaffinized, rehydrated, and stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) to visualize tissue architecture and identify germinal centers under the EVOS fluorescence microscope.

Germinal center counts and areas were quantified using ImageJ software, with areas calibrated to a 2mm reference scale on each slide. Statistical comparisons were performed using one- and two-tailed t-tests in Jupyter Notebook.

EVOS Microscope Images — H&E Stained Spleen Tissue

Figure 1 — H&E Stained Spleen Samples

Spleen samples from all four mice after hematoxylin and eosin staining, imaged under the EVOS microscope. Samples 1 and 2 are from uninjured mice; Samples 3 and 4 are from mice with chronic pain.

  • Hematoxylin stains nuclei blue/purple; Eosin stains other tissue pink
  • Injured samples (3 & 4) appear noticeably darker, indicating increased immune activity
  • Visual differences in tissue density are observable between the two groups

Figure 2 — Germinal Centers Identified (Circled)

The same four stained spleen samples with a germinal center circled in each image to guide identification. Germinal centers are regions within the spleen where B cells actively proliferate and generate antibody responses.

  • Germinal centers appear as lighter, rounded structures within the darker lymphoid tissue
  • Injured mice show visibly larger and more numerous germinal centers
  • This suggests chronic pain triggers an elevated adaptive immune response in the spleen
Quantitative Results

Figure 3 — Quantity of Germinal Centers per Mouse

Raw counts of germinal centers identified in each mouse's spleen tissue. Injured mice (3 & 4) show substantially higher germinal center counts compared to uninjured controls (1 & 2).

  • Mouse 3 (injured) had the highest count at ~40 germinal centers
  • Mouse 4 (injured) had ~35 germinal centers
  • Uninjured mice had significantly fewer, suggesting chronic pain drives expanded immune activity

Figure 4 — Germinal Center Areas: Injured vs. Uninjured Mice

Average germinal center area (mm²) per mouse, quantified using ImageJ software. Area was calibrated to a 2mm reference scale on each slide.

  • Injured mice (3 & 4) showed germinal center areas of ~0.40 mm² and ~0.33 mm²
  • Uninjured mice had areas of ~0.12 mm² and ~0.06 mm² — 3–6x smaller
  • Larger germinal centers in injured mice reflect more active B cell proliferation in response to chronic pain signaling
Measurement Method — ImageJ

Area Quantification via ImageJ Software

Germinal center areas were measured by tracing each center using the ellipse selection tool in ImageJ. The pixel scale was calibrated using the 2mm reference marker printed on each slide.

Uninjured mouse (Mouse 1) — smaller germinal center

Injured mouse (Mouse 3) — visibly larger germinal center

Key Findings

Injured mice had 3–6× larger germinal center areas than uninjured controls.
Chronic pain appears to significantly elevate adaptive immune activity in the spleen.
H&E staining revealed visibly darker tissue in injured samples, consistent with increased cellularity.
Results suggest the spleen plays an active role in the immune response to chronic pain signaling.

Study Design

4 male mice total — 2 uninjured (saline injection control) and 2 injured (MIA chronic pain model). Spleens dissected, processed through histology, stained, and imaged across multiple tissue sections per animal.
